name: BRCA1 & BRCA2 DEL/DUP ANALYSIS BY MLPA

data.value:
CLINICAL HISTORY

A 50-year-old female was referred for the genetic evaluation of BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes.

Clinical Indication: Triple negative breast cancer (TNBC)

Clinical suspicion: Hereditary breast cancer

Family HIstory: Not provided.

TEST CHARACTERISTICS

Copy number changes in 24 exons of the BRCA1 and 27 exons of BRCA2 genes are identified by hybridizing
with MLPA (Multiplex Ligation-dependent Probe Amplification) based assay.

TEST RESULTS AND INTERPRETATION

NO DELETION OR DUPLICATION DETECTED IN BRCA1 & BRCA2 GENES
(Fig:1&2 in Appendix 1)

SUMMARY

BRCA1 and BRCA2 are responsible for accurate DNA repair of double‐strand breaks. In addition to the compromised DNA repair function, mutations in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes are likely to affect cell cycle regulation and  transcriptional activity. More than 1,800 pathogenic variants has been reported in BRCA1 and BRCA2 gene which are associated with an increased risk of breast cancer, ovarian cancer, fallopian tube, prostate cancer, pancreatic cancer and melanoma. BRCA1 & BRCA2 genes account for about 20 to 25% of hereditary breast cancers and about 5 to 10% of all breast cancers. In addition, mutations in the BRCA1 & BRCA2 genes account for around 15% of ovarian cancers overall. Most of the reported BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations are characterized by deletions, insertions, nonsense  mutations, splice variants and an increasing number of large genomic rearrangements. Analysis for large genomic rearrangements which includes large deletion/duplication in BRCA1 & BRCA2 provides an efficient diagnosis for this disorder in individual with a family history of BRCA1 & BRCA2 related disorders.

For this patient, no deletions or duplications were detected in abnormal range, within the detection limits of MLPA, in the BRCA1 & BRCA2 genes (Fig: 1 & 2).

RECOMMENDATION

  • Genetic counseling is advised.
  • BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes sequencing via NGS.

Technical Note
Methodology

Copy number changes in targeted regions of the BRCA1 (24 exons) & BRCA2 (27 exons) genes were identified by hybridizing with MLPA (Multiplex Ligation dependent Probe Amplification) probes. Each MLPA probe consists of two hemi-probes that bind to adjacent sites on the target sequence. Upon ligation and subsequent PCR amplification, each distinct MLPA probe (specific to distinct target regions) generates an amplicon with a unique length which are separated and quantified by capillary electrophoresis. Heterozygous deletions within target sequences will prevent efficient probe binding and give a 35-50% reduced relative peak area of the amplification product specific to that probe set. Copy number differences of various exons between test and control DNA samples can be detected by analyzing the MLPA peak patterns. The use of these assays as a stand-alone test without previous NGS sequencing is not recommended as this can lead to misinterpretation of test results.

LIMITATIONS 

  •  The MLPA test will not detect the point mutations in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes, which accounts for most of genetic defects. It is therefore recommended to use MLPA in combination with sequence analysis.  
  • A point mutation or polymorphism in the sequence detected by a probe, which results in reduced probe binding efficiency, can also cause a reduction in relative peak area. Therefore, single exon deletions detected by MLPA should always be confirmed by other methods like multiplex PCR or sequencing. 
  •  MLPA cannot detect any changes that lie outside the target sequence of the probes and will not detect most inversions or  translocations. Even when MLPA did not detect any aberrations, the possibility remains that biological  changes in that gene or chromosomal region do exist but remain undetected.                     
  • Although all precautions are taken during Molecular Genetic testing the currently available data indicate that the technical error rate for all types of Molecular DNA analysis is approximately 2%.
  • This test has not been validated by the FDA, NABL or CAP, and it has been determined by the accrediting bodies that such validation is not required at this time. This report is for research purposes only, not for use in clinical diagnostic or therapeutic applications.
